string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and an important centre of government, history, education, and culture. Located in northern China, it has served as a capital during several periods of Chinese history. The Forbidden City was home to imperial courts, while the Temple of Heaven and the Summer Palace reflect the art and architecture of earlier dynasties. Famous sections of the Great Wall lie outside the urban centre. Today, Beijing combines historic neighbourhoods with modern business districts, universities, museums, and extensive public transport. Visitors can explore traditional hutong streets, major public squares, parks, and a wide range of cultural attractions.

Shanghai is a major city on the eastern coast of China, located near the mouth of the Yangtze River. The Huangpu River divides prominent central areas, including the historic Bund and the modern skyline of Pudong. Shanghai developed as an important trading port and remains a significant centre for finance, shipping, commerce, and culture. Its streets feature a mix of historic architecture, contemporary towers, museums, and busy shopping areas. Public transport connects many neighbourhoods across the city. Shanghai is also known for its food, creative industries, and waterfront views, reflecting both its long commercial history and its continuing urban development.

Chongqing is a direct-administered municipality in southwestern China, known for its mountainous landscape and dramatic river scenery. The Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet near its urban centre, and numerous bridges connect neighbourhoods built across steep hills. Chongqing has long been important for inland transport, trade, and industry. Its busy streets, high-rise buildings, and riverside districts form a distinctive cityscape. The region is also associated with the Three Gorges along the Yangtze River. Local cuisine is famous for bold, spicy flavours, especially Chongqing hot pot. Traditional communities, modern development, and surrounding natural landscapes all contribute to its distinctive character.

Tianjin is a direct-administered municipality in northern China, situated near the Bohai Sea and closely connected to Beijing. The city developed as an important port and trading centre, while the Hai River runs through its urban areas. Parts of Tianjin contain architecture influenced by periods of international trade, including buildings around the Five Great Avenues. Popular landmarks include the Tianjin Eye observation wheel and Ancient Culture Street. Today, Tianjin plays a major role in manufacturing, shipping, education, and regional transport. Its museums, riverside views, traditional markets, and local foods offer visitors a mixture of historical and modern urban experiences.
